newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong activists throw down democracy gauntlet.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong activists throw down democracy gauntlet.

text.p: Hong Kong activists marched on Tuesday in a challenge to their new Chinese-picked leaders to restore democracy, while Beijing trod softly, pledging never to put troops on the streets in armoured cars.

"We want democracy. We want it now," demonstrators chanted on the first day of Hong Kong's rule by China, which signalled its sovereignty by sending in 4,000 People's Liberation Army troops backed by armour.

The protest by several thousand marchers was the largest of several early challenges to the new leadership under shipping billionaire Tung Chee-hwa, which took over from the British after midnight on Monday.
Pro-democracy activists regard the arrival of PLA forces, and particularly armoured cars, as a provocative reminder of the 1989 Tiananmen massacre of demonstrators in Beijing.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen "has explicitly confirmed that the defence role of the PLA is solely external, not internal.
"Chinese troops should not be seen in marches or in armoured personnel carriers on the streets of Hong Kong," he told reporters after meeting Qian.
Tung reinforced the assurances from Beijing.
"Democracy is the hallmark of a new era for Hong Kong," he said in a speech outlining his economic and social agenda.
While noisy demonstrators marched through Hong Kong's Central business district, other residents offered a warmer response to embrace by the motherland.
In the semi-rural New Territories, Chinese troops who arrived in lashing rain -- standing stiffly to attention on the backs of open trucks -- were cheered and clapped by thousands of wellwishers.
The stern gazes and stiff waves of the soldiers were answered by smiles from onlookers who offered garlands, flowers and welcome penants.

Cook said he also won assurances from Qian elections would be held in Hong Kong by next May. The old democratically-elected legislature was dissolved at midnight and a new Beijing-picked assembly sworn in.
Tung had already named May as the election date.

Elite units of the PLA swarmed into the territory through drenching rain at dawn, crossing the border at three points to garrison the new Special Adminstrative Region, which has been promised wide autonomy for the next 50 years.
A flotilla of warships churned towards the new naval base at Stonecutters island. Helicopters roared across the frontier carrying more troops.

Although the display of military force has drawn expressions of unease from Britain and the United States, Beijing views it as a joyous affirmation of sovereignty after a century and a half of colonial shame.
The iron fist was wrapped in a velvet glove when China's President Jiang Zemin pledged that this East Asian economic hub would remain economically powerful with autonomy and existing freedoms.
His wide-ranging speech, upholding the private enterprise and investment which underpins Hong Kong's success, was clearly aimed at easing anxieties and signalling business as usual.
China wants to see its new region "forever vigorous and dynamic".
Declaring Hong Kong must remain "the world's freest and most vibrant economy", Tung unveiled a bold policy agenda for China's latest and richest region.
He pledged action to bring down the astronomical cost of housing, improve educational opportunities at overcrowded schools and take steps to upgrade Hong Kong's technological base.
Tuesday's march by the Alliance in Support of Democratic Patriotic Movements in China stretched for more than a kilometre (half a mile), snarling traffic in the city centre.
Onlookers enjoying the national holiday stopped to watch and people packed overhead foot bridges to get a better view.

The protesters carried banners demanding the restoration of political reforms introduced in the twilight of British rule. Tung has curbed the right to protest and restricted foreign funding for political parties.
One marcher, Anthea Ho, 27, said she was in the protest because she feared democracy would die out in Hong Kong under Chinese rule.
"Hong Kong doesn't have enough democracy now, and if we go backwards, we'll have even less," Ho said.
Cheung Chi-kwong, 50, a factory-owner, said: "Now many pro-democracy supporters are still being persecuted. Why can this happen? We must fight it now."
Police turned out in force, but the march was peaceful and orderly.
In future, protesters will have to obtain permits from police before marching. But for the first two days of Chinese rule they needed only to inform police of their plans.
